title: Spin Hall Magnetoresistance in Antiferromagnetic Insulators
authors: Stephan Geprägs, Matthias Opel, Johanna Fischer, Philipp Schwenke, Matthias Althammer, Hans Huebl, Rudolf Gross
abstract: Antiferromagnetic materials promise improved performance for spintronic applications, as they are robust against external magnetic field perturbations and allow for faster magnetization dynamics compared to ferromagnets. The direct observation of the antiferromagnetic state, however, is challenging due to the absence of a macroscopic magnetization. We show that the spin Hall magnetoresistance (SMR) is a versatile tool to probe the antiferromagnetic spin structure via simple electrical transport experiments by investigating the easy-plane antiferromagnetic insulators alpha-Fe2O3 (hematite) and NiO in bilayer heterostructures with a Pt heavy-metal top electrode. While rotating an external magnetic field in three orthogonal planes, we record the longitudinal and the transverse resistivities of Pt and observe characteristic resistivity modulations consistent with the SMR effect. We analyze both their amplitude and phase and compare the data to the results from a prototypical collinear ferrimagnetic Y3Fe5O12/Pt bilayer. The observed magnetic field dependence is explained in a comprehensive model, based on two magnetic sublattices and taking into account magnetic field-induced modifications of the domain structure. Our results show that the SMR effect allows to readout the spin configuration and to investigate magnetoelastic effects in antiferromagnetic multi-domain materials. We demonstrate that the SMR amplitude scales with the sum of the absolute sublattice magnetizations in ferrimagnetic and antiferromagnetic materials. In alpha-Fe2O3/Pt bilayers, we find an unexpectedly large SMR amplitude of 2.5E-3, twice as high as for prototype Y3Fe5O12/Pt bilayers, making the system particularly interesting for room-temperature antiferromagnetic spintronic applications.
summary: This work demonstrates that the Spin Hall Magnetoresistance (SMR) effect is a powerful, non-invasive tool for characterizing the spin structure of antiferromagnetic insulators. By measuring resistivity changes under rotating magnetic fields, the authors show that the SMR amplitude scales predictably with the sublattice magnetization, allowing for the study of AF spintronics in materials like $\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$. This provides a robust method for reading out magnetic order in systems previously difficult to probe.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a simple electrical transport method to probe the spin structure of antiferromagnetic (AF) materials, which lack a net macroscopic magnetization.
main_result: The Spin Hall Magnetoresistance (SMR) effect successfully reads out the spin configuration in AF insulators, showing that the SMR amplitude scales with the sum of absolute sublattice magnetizations.
method: Angle-dependent magnetoresistance (ADMR) measurements are performed by measuring the longitudinal and transverse resistivities of a Pt top electrode as an external magnetic field is rotated in-plane.
model_or_system: The study uses bilayer heterostructures combining easy-plane antiferromagnetic insulators (like $\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ and NiO) with a Pt heavy-metal electrode. The analysis is modeled using two magnetic sublattices ($M_A$ and $M_B$) and comparing results to known ferrimagnetic systems.
key_observables: Characteristic sinusoidal modulations in longitudinal and transverse resistivities ($\rho_{long}$ and $\rho_{trans}$), and the SMR amplitude.
important_parameters: The SMR amplitude scales with the product of the volume density ($n$) of magnetic ions and their spin state ($S$), i.e., $nS$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the SMR effect is sensitive to the spin configuration of *all* independent magnetic sublattices, not just the net magnetization.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows in-plane ADMR for $\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$/Pt, NiO/Pt, and Y$_3$Fe$_5$O$_{12}$/Pt bilayers. Figure 2 illustrates the scaling behavior of the maximum SMR.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (probing AF spin structure) by introducing SMR as a tool. It details the measurements on various bilayers, develops a comprehensive model based on two sublattices, and presents results showing the universal scaling of the SMR amplitude with $nS$.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the use of electrical transport to map out complex, non-collinear magnetic order parameters is relevant to understanding quantum states in engineered materials, bridging classical magnetism with transport physics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. In-plane ADMR at 300 K in a magnetic field of 7 T of antiferromagnetic (0001)-oriented α-Fe2O3/Pt (blue) and (111)-oriented NiO/Pt (red) bilayers as well as a ferrimagnetic (001)-oriented Y3Fe5O12 (YIG)/Pt bilayer (black). The symbols represent the normalized (a) longitudinal (ρlong) and (b) transverse (ρtrans) resistivities measured while rotating the magnetic field in the film plane. The data are plotted as a function of the magnetic field orientation α. The lines are fits to the data using cos 2α and sin 2α functions.

Fig. 2. Scaling behavior of the maximum SMR amplitude ρ1/ρ0 at 300 K from different FMI/Pt [2] or AFI/Pt [4,5] samples with a Pt thickness of 3 nm. The values are plotted versus the product of the spin S of the magnetic ions times their volume density n in the “bulk” of the FMI or AFI. The dashed blue line is a guide to the eye. While the phase of ρlong and ρtrans is well understood, the amplitudes ρ1/ρ0 and ρ3/ρ0 are a matter of debate. Our epitaxial, antiferromagnetic α-Fe2O3 thin films implemented in a heterostructure with a 3 nm thin Pt electrode show the highest SMR amplitudes reported in literature so far [4].
